360394f33e3e2f99029aa4cd8fae22bad3ef8ae2.summary: An Eclectic Light article, published 2020-11-16, sets out a first draft of how macOS 10.15 and 11.0 check executable code before loading and running it. It covers code signing on Intel and Apple Silicon Macs, a local security database of code hashes, hash lookups sent to Apple, and online developer certificate revocation checks. The author says Apple has stated its privacy position and plans to add an opt-out. The article names no specific malware family, campaign, vulnerability or incident.

hedges: This is my first draft, so please bear with my errors and help me correct them to build a more accurate picture.
This has been thought to relate to notarization, but I don't think has anything to do with that.
At the least, Apple collects hashes as they're encountered, and appears to look them up in a database of known malware.
Apple appears to have changed this system over a year ago.
This appears to have been extended to 12 hours now.
For a very few Mac users, such as journalists who work in hostile environments, the OCSP exchange and transmission of new hashes could conceivably be used against them.
Apple's statement that the new opt-out preference presumably means both hash lookup and certificate revocation checks is the author's inference.

36306e003905c18244827376abe525ad46e1a655.summary: Microsoft threat analysts linked the financially motivated group FIN7, also tracked as Sangria Tempest, to an April 2023 campaign deploying Clop ransomware. The attacks used the POWERTRASH dropper and the Lizar tool, with OpenSSH and Impacket for lateral movement. Microsoft also linked FIN7 to PaperCut printing server attacks using Clop, Bl00dy and LockBit, and tied FIN11 (Lace Tempest) to FIN7 tooling. The article recounts FIN7's history since 2013, including attacks on banks and point-of-sale terminals, USB lures, and prison sentences for several members in 2021 and 2022.

3647d0b1f55f78d0fd793ebc76728e2aecddd9f0.summary: The page is titled as a report on PolinRider, described as a DPRK threat actor implanting malware in hundreds of GitHub repositories. The body contains no analysis. It is a long numbered list of repository names, owners and project descriptions, with no malware behaviour, attribution, activity dates or indicators stated. It is classified as not a threat report because it is an index.
